Q: Why is Rust's sort much faster than C++'s std::sort? A:

I compiled the C++ using /opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/clang++ -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto -funroll-loops -fomit-frame-pointer -DNDEBUG -fexperimental-library KimBomm.cpp and changed the sort line in the code to std::sort(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end());.

The C++ version ran 60% faster than the Rust version.

Q: Applying custom segmented function to a subarray in jax A:

For a non-element-wise function as in the user's question, I don't know of any good way to do this, short of masking out the array outside JIT where vec_masked = vec[mask] can be constructed without issue. Over the years the JAX team has explored some possible implementations of dynamic-shaped or ragged arrays within JIT, but none is currently mature enough to be used in the general case.

For the simpler case of an element-wise function, the recommended way to do this is using the three-term jnp.where:

@jax.jit
def func_segmented(vec, mask):
    return jnp.where(mask, vec_fun(vec), vec)

The downside of this is that vec_fun is computed on the full vector, so it includes some wasted computation. The benefit of this is that it's trivially vectorizable (and parallelizable if running on accelerators) and the sizes of arrays don't depend on runtime values so no new compilation is necessary when values within the mask change.

If you believe it's important to avoid wasted the wasted computation of this approach, your best options are either

  1. statically split your vector outside JIT and pass just the desired portion to vec_fun. The downside here is that this must be done outside JIT, and vec_fun would be recompiled for each new size, which may overshadow gains from avoiding wasted computation.

  2. Use lax.map to sequentially iterate over your array (or chunks of your array, with the batch_size parameter) and call-out to vec_fun only when needed. The benefit here is less wasted computation, but the downside is that the cost of sequential computation can overshadow any improvements.

If runtime cost is important, you might benchmark these three options. But in general the jnp.where approach (which trades wasted computation for ability to run in parallel without recompilation) tends to be the most performant.

Q: Firebase Storage Bucket Domain Shows " firebasestorage.app " Instead of " appspot.com " A:

There were changes to the product that you need to be aware of. Neither of your expectations are valid now.

Firebase Storage is no longer available on the free tier. You must upgrade to use it. See the documentation:

Important: The following changes to pricing plan requirements are happening for Cloud Storage for Firebase. Learn more in the FAQs.

  • Starting October 30, 2024, your Firebase project must be on the pay-as-you-go Blaze pricing plan to provision a new Cloud Storage for Firebase default bucket. The bucket can optionally use the "Always Free" tier for Google Cloud Storage.

  • Starting October 1, 2025, your Firebase project must be on the pay-as-you-go Blaze pricing plan to maintain access to your default bucket and all other Cloud Storage resources. Any *.appspot.com default bucket will maintain its current no-cost level of usage even on the Blaze pricing plan.

See also:

  • Firebase cloud storage ( for projects)

The name of the buckets have changed. This is also covered in the documentation:

Note: Starting October 30, 2024, all new default Cloud Storage buckets have the name format PROJECT_ID.firebasestorage.app. Any default buckets created before that date have the name format PROJECT_ID.appspot.com. Learn more in the FAQs.

If you click through to the FAQs, you will read:

Important: Here are the summarized key points of the FAQs in this section (but make sure to review each FAQ below for details):

  • Starting October 30, 2024, all newly provisioned default Cloud Storage buckets will have the name format of PROJECT_ID.firebasestorage.app.
  • These buckets will follow Google Cloud Storage pricing and usage, which provides an "Always Free" tier for buckets in US-CENTRAL1, US-EAST1, and US-WEST1.
  • There are no changes to any existing PROJECT_ID.appspot.com default buckets (as long as you upgrade your project to the pay-as-you-go Blaze pricing plan by October 1, 2025).

You can still use the product for free up to the documented limits, but your project must be on a payment plan so that it can be billed for any overages.

Q: Xcode 26.4 build error: "call to consteval function 'fmt::basic_format_string' is not a constant expression" in React Native iOS build A:

Fix for Xcode 26.4 / C++20 build errors in React Native

The new compiler in Xcode 26.4 changed how it handles C++20 features. It’s now rejecting the way the older {fmt} library (included in React Native) validates strings at compile-time.

The easiest fix is to force the fmt library to use C++17 instead of C++20. Since consteval didn't exist in C++17, the compiler will stop complaining and the build will succeed.

Add this to your ios/Podfile inside the post_install block:

post_install do |installer|
  # Keep your existing react_native_post_install here
  react_native_post_install(installer, config[:reactNativePath])

  # Fix for Xcode 26.4 build error
  installer.pods_project.targets.each do |target|
    if target.name == 'fmt'
      target.build_configurations.each do |config|
        config.build_settings['CLANG_CXX_LANGUAGE_STANDARD'] = 'c++17'
      end
    end
  end
end

Why this works: We only target the fmt library specifically. You shouldn't change the whole project to C++17 because other parts of React Native actually need C++20 to run.

To apply:

  1. Save the Podfile.

  2. Run pod install in your terminal.

  3. Clean your build in Xcode and run it again.
